content.title: Cardiology fellowship launched in Nairobi
content.summary: AKU's new programme will develop heart specialists with life-saving skills.

content.text: Aga Khan University's teaching hospital in Nairobi has launched the region's

The new three-year programme, which is being managed by the Department of Postgraduate Medical Education, will enable Kenyan physicians to gain advanced knowledge and skills in the clinical, diagnostic and interventional areas of the specialty without having to leave the country.

"This is the first recognised fellowship programme in cardiology in the region," said Dr Mohamed Jeilan, director of cardiology services at AKUH Nairobi (AKUH N). "Its uniqueness stems from the fact that our fellows undergo a structured and curriculum-based programme that models them into a well-rounded cardiologist that can deliver care to patients in a dynamic and challenging environment in Africa."

The programme will see fellows undergo rotations in five core areas of practice: imaging, cardiac catheterization, inpatient and outpatient care, and research. The fellowship has been tailored to meet local needs and will help create specialists who can deal with the rising threat of cardiovascular diseases in the country .

Kenya has around 40 cardiologists for its population of 48 million people, according to Dr Mzee Ngunga, director of the cardiology fellowship and an assistant professor in the department of medicine at Aga Khan University. Most of these specialists practice in Nairobi or the cities of Kisumu and Mombasa which means that most Kenyans have to travel long distances to access quality care.

Dr Ngunga said: "For the first time in Kenya, we are now able to train cardiologists to conduct complex procedures in heart medicine, including implantation of heart devices and procedures related to haemodynamic monitoring in very sick patients.

"Training is hands-on with a dedicated team of consultant cardiologists who are widely involved in research to improve existing care models and innovations in methods of care delivery," Dr Ngunga added.
Three fellows are currently enrolled in the programme with a fourth expected to join in mid-2018.

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of death around the world, according to the World Health Organization. Targets under goal 3 of the Sustainable Development Goals: ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages, call for a one-third reduction in the mortality rate from CVDs through steps to enhance treatment and preventive care.
